walkthroughs.body_html:
3.4 x 10^5 means 340000.

Keep one non-zero digit before the point.

For a ruler reading to 1 mm: uncertainty +- 0.5 mm.

% uncertainty = (uncertainty / measurement) x 100.

mcqs.q: After one half-life, what happens to an individual radioactive nucleus?
options: Every nucleus is guaranteed to have half-decayed after one half-life.
Yes — it was a bomb-like event that destroyed an earlier universe.
The nucleus shrinks to half its original size after one half-life.
It has a 50 percent chance of having decayed — radioactive decay is random for any single nucleus.

mcqs.q: Is radioactive decay periodic — does each nucleus decay at regular intervals?
options: Yes — it was a bomb-like event that destroyed an earlier universe.
No — decay is a random process; half-life is a statistical property of a large population.
Yes — half-life is the time between each emission from the source.
Yes — each nucleus 'ticks' at intervals of one half-life until it decays.

mcqs.q: Was the Big Bang an explosion of matter into pre-existing space?
options: Yes — it was a bomb-like event that destroyed an earlier universe.
Yes — it was a giant explosion at a point, and galaxies are still flying outwards from it.
The nucleus shrinks to half its original size after one half-life.
No — it was the expansion of space itself, beginning from a hot dense state; there was no 'outside' for matter to expand into.
